McLaren.summary: McLaren’s package this weekend features a re‑shaped floor that smooths the airflow under the car, giving a boost in down‑force and better grip through the corners. The revised rear‑suspension fairing and a fresh rear‑wing design both tighten up the rear‑end aerodynamics, helping the car stick to the track on acceleration and braking. Together, these tweaks should translate into quicker lap times and a more stable ride, especially on high‑speed sections.

Mercedes F1 Team.summary: Mercedes has reshaped the R01’s sidepods to push more air down the car and added a higher‑placed inlet, while the front and rear wings now sit at a steeper angle and the front wing lost its little “fins”. The net effect is more grip and a tighter, more responsive feel through the corners, giving the team a better chance to attack on this weekend’s twisty layout. In short, the car should be stickier and easier to drive, which could translate into higher qualifying positions and more battles on track.

Racing Bulls / RB.summary: Racing Bulls have re‑shaped their car to meet the new 2026 rules, most noticeably with a slimmer, longer front wing that works better with the SM‑system and a three‑element active rear wing that can give a bigger boost on the straights. The under‑body has been trimmed down – a simpler floor, a reshaped engine‑cover deck and refreshed rear‑corner winglets – all aimed at cleaning up airflow and keeping the tyres in the right temperature window, while circuit‑specific cooling‑louvre tweaks help the power unit stay happy. In short, the package should be more aerodynamically efficient and easier to manage, giving RB a better chance to attack the front of the grid this weekend.

Aston Martin.summary: Aston Martin has slimmed out the front with a three‑element narrow wing and a new dive‑plane endplate, giving the car a sharper bite into corners and more stability under braking. Raising the nose and moving the side‑pod inlet higher opens up airflow, while the reshaped engine cover and diffuser keep that air glued to the floor for extra rear grip, and a three‑element rear wing with fresh pylons adds down‑force where it matters most. Together these changes should boost straight‑line speed and cornering confidence, helping the team fight for better lap times this weekend.

Haas F1 Team.summary: Haas has tweaked three key aero pieces for 2026: the diffuser now has a fresh shape that lets the car generate a little more rear‑end grip, the upper rear wing has been switched to a three‑element layout (but within a tighter volume), and the lower “beam” wing has been stripped back to a simple single element. These changes mean the car should be more stable through high‑speed corners and have a cleaner aerodynamic balance, giving Haas a better chance to attack the front of the grid this weekend.

Alpine F1 Team.summary: Alpine has rolled out a brand‑new front wing, rear wing and engine‑cover package that meets the fresh 2026 aero rules, giving the car a cleaner, more efficient shape. The updated wings should boost grip in corners and keep the car stable under braking, while the new engine‑cover smooths the airflow to help the car pull harder on the straights. In short, the changes are aimed at making the car feel more planted and quicker this weekend, giving Alpine a better shot at fighting up the grid.

Audi F1 Team.summary: Audi’s new front wing now has an independent actuator on each side, letting the team fine‑tune the airflow on the left and right separately for better grip in corners. The side‑pod inlet has been reshaped to work hand‑in‑hand with the floor and rear body, while the upper side‑pod surface now slopes downward, cleaning up turbulent “down‑wash” and feeding smoother air to the rear. Together these tweaks give the car a tighter, more stable aerodynamic package, which should translate into higher corner speeds and stronger tyre performance right out of the box for this weekend’s race.

Cadillac.summary: Cadillac’s aero package got a quick refresh: the front wing flaps and endplates have been reshaped to spread the load more evenly, and the rear wing’s flaps have been tweaked for a smoother bite. Those tweaks give the car tighter front‑end grip and more stable rear‑end push, translating into better corner‑entry confidence and faster lap times this weekend. In short, the car should feel more planted and easier to drive around the track.
